analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security cost-of-living increases for seniors and extends the payroll tax to all high wages.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final month of the 112th Congress with zero cosponsors; the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change Social Security in two main ways. First, it would create a new inflation index built around what people 62 and older actually buy, and use it to calculate annual benefit increases for seniors, whose costs (especially health care) rise faster than the general index. Second, it would gradually lift the cap that exempts wages above a certain level from the Social Security payroll tax, so by 2019 every dollar of wages and self-employment income would be taxed, with a small portion of that extra money returned to high earners as slightly higher benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors age 62 and older collecting Social Security would get larger annual cost-of-living increases matched to their actual expenses. The program's trust funds would also gain revenue, extending solvency. Low- and middle-income workers pay nothing additional, since the tax applies only to income above the annual wage cap.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a monthly Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers tracking spending typical of people 62 or older, and makes that index the basis for cost-of-living increases in benefits for anyone 62 or older [S2][S3].

Phases out the exemption for wages above the Social Security contribution and benefit base: 86% of above-cap wages count in 2013, declining each year until 100% of wages are subject to the tax after 2018, with the same phase-in for self-employment income [S2][S3].

Counts earnings above the old cap as 'surplus earnings' in the benefit formula, giving high earners a modest benefit increase (a 3% and 0.25% factor on surplus earnings) as partial offset for the new taxes they pay [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners — employees and especially self-employed people whose wages or net earnings exceed the annual Social Security wage cap — would pay Social Security tax on income currently exempt, up to the full combined rate by 2019. Higher benefit payouts from the new elderly index would be paid for largely by this new revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: The phase-in table would subject all wages and self-employment income above the annual cap to the payroll tax after 2018, a tax increase falling on high-income workers and business owners, who pay both the employee and employer shares on self-employment income [S3].

A good-faith objection to lifting the cap is that Social Security has always tied benefits to taxed contributions; the bill partially preserves that link by paying high earners somewhat higher benefits on their surplus earnings, but only at low rates (3% and 0.25%), so most new revenue does not buy proportional benefits [S3].

Switching seniors to an elderly-specific price index would raise benefit costs permanently; the bill's solvency math depends on the new tax revenue outpacing those higher payouts, which an honest supporter would acknowledge is a long-run projection, not a guarantee [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and targeted: seniors, whose real costs often rise faster than the headline inflation index, would see their benefits keep pace better, and the program gains a dedicated revenue stream. The cost is real but concentrated: a phased tax increase on income above the wage cap, softened slightly by modest benefit credits for those same high earners. The design is straightforward rather than gimmicky — a bigger benefit paid for by broader taxation — but its long-run solvency effects depend on projections the bill itself cannot guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in December 2012 and the committee never took it up before the 112th Congress ended three weeks later, so it died with no vote and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Begich introduced the bill on December 4, 2012, in the final weeks of the 112th Congress [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, which was its last action of record [S5].
No senator cosponsored the bill [S4], and the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 without the committee or the full Senate ever considering it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the Social Security wage cap are better off, since they never faced the new tax on income above the cap. Seniors gained nothing, as the higher cost-of-living increases never arrived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the wage cap

for.name: Sen. Mark Begich
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alaska; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 4, 2012, in the Senate's final weeks and it was referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Max Baucus)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no committee action after the referral.

against.name: 112th Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill; it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measurable support or opposition from either party [S4][S5].

industries.industry: High earners above the Social Security wage cap
industries.note: The bill would phase in Social Security taxation on all wages and self-employment income above the annual cap, reaching 100% after 2018, in exchange for only a small benefit increase for those same earners. The revenue funds larger benefits for seniors, so this group's interest runs against the bill's gain for beneficiaries.

Self-employment income above the cap would be taxed under the same phase-in, and the self-employed bear both the employee and employer shares of the payroll tax, making this the largest per-dollar cost of the bill.
